danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: Da Jermolov (Kutuzovs udsending), der var blevet sendt af Kutuzov for at inspicere stillingen, fortalte feltmarskalken, at det var umuligt at kæmpe dér foran Moskva, og at de måtte trække sig tilbage, så Kutuzov på ham i tavshed.
»Giv mig din hånd,« sagde han og vendte den om for at mærke pulsen, og tilføjede: »Du er ikke rask, min kære ven. Tænk over, hvad du siger!«
Kutuzov kunne endnu ikke indrømme muligheden af at trække sig tilbage bag Moskva uden slag.

På Poklonnij-højen, fire mil fra Dorogomilov-porten i Moskva, steg Kutuzov ud af sin vogn og satte sig på en bænk ved vejkanten. En stor skare generaler samledes omkring ham, og grev Rostoptjin, der var kommet ud fra Moskva, sluttede sig til dem. Dette glimrende selskab delte sig i flere grupper, der alle drøftede stillingens fordele og ulemper, hærens tilstand, de foreslåede planer, Moskvas situation og militære spørgsmål i almindelighed. Skønt de ikke var indkaldt til formålet, og skønt det ikke blev kaldt det, følte de alle, at dette i virkeligheden var et krigsråd. Samtalerne drejede sig alle om offentlige anliggender. Hvis nogen gav eller spurgte efter personlige nyheder, skete det hviskende, og de vendte straks tilbage til de almene spørgsmål. Ingen vittigheder, latter eller smil var at se blandt alle disse mænd. De bestræbte sig tydeligvis alle på at holde sig på højde med situationens alvor. Og alle disse grupper forsøgte, mens de talte indbyrdes, at holde sig nær øverstkommanderende (hvis bænk udgjorde midtpunktet for forsamlingen) og at tale, så han kunne høre dem. Øverstkommanderende lyttede til, hvad der blev sagt, og bad sommetider om at få bemærkninger gentaget, men deltog ikke selv i samtalerne og udtrykte ingen holdning. Efter at have hørt, hvad der blev sagt i den ene eller den anden af disse grupper, vendte han sig som regel bort med et skuffet udtryk, som om de ikke talte om noget, han ønskede at høre. Nogle drøftede den stilling, der var blevet valgt, og kritiserede ikke så meget selve stillingen som den intellektuelle kapacitet hos dem, der havde valgt den. Andre hævdede, at der var begået en fejl tidligere, og at et slag burde have været leveret to dage forinden. Andre igen talte om slaget ved Salamanca, som blev beskrevet af Crosart, en nyankommet franskmand i spansk uniform. (Denne franskmand og en af de tyske prinser, der tjente i den russiske hær, diskuterede belejringen af Zaragoza og overvejede muligheden for at forsvare Moskva på lignende vis.) Grev Rostoptjin fortalte en fjerde gruppe, at han var rede til at dø med byens borgermilits under hovedstadens mure, men at han alligevel ikke kunne lade være med at beklage, at han var holdt i uvidenhed om, hvad der foregik, og at hvis han havde vidst det tidligere, ville tingene have set anderledes ud... En femte gruppe, der fremviste dybden af deres strategiske indsigt, drøftede den retning, tropperne nu måtte tage. En sjette gruppe talte rent vrøvl. Kutuzovs udtryk blev mere og mere bekymret og dystert. Af al denne snak så han kun én ting: at forsvare Moskva var en fysisk umulighed i ordets fulde betydning, det vil sige, så aldeles umuligt, at hvis en meningsløs kommandant gav ordre til kamp, ville resultatet blive forvirring, men slaget ville alligevel ikke finde sted. Det ville ikke finde sted, fordi alle kommandanterne ikke blot anerkendte stillingen som umulig, men i deres samtaler kun drøftede, hvad der ville ske efter dens uundgåelige opgivelse. Hvordan skulle kommandanterne føre deres tropper til en slagmark, de anså for umulig at holde? De lavere officerer og selv soldaterne (der også ræsonnerer) anså ligeledes stillingen for umulig og kunne derfor ikke gå i kamp, fuldt overbeviste som de var om nederlaget. Hvis Bennigsen insisterede på at forsvare stillingen, og andre stadig drøftede den, var spørgsmålet ikke længere vigtigt i sig selv, men kun som påskud for stridigheder og intriger. Det vidste Kutuzov godt.

Bennigsen, der havde valgt stillingen, fremviste varmt sin russiske patriotisme (Kutuzov kunne ikke lytte til dette uden at krympe sig) ved at insistere på, at Moskva måtte forsvares. Hans hensigt var klar som dag for Kutuzov: hvis forsvaret mislykkedes, at kaste skylden på Kutuzov, der havde ført hæren helt til Spurvebakkerne uden at levere slag; hvis det lykkedes, at tage æren for det; eller hvis der ikke blev kæmpet, at rense sig for forbrydelsen med at opgive Moskva. Men denne intrige optog ikke længere den gamle mands sind. Ét frygteligt spørgsmål opslugte ham, og det spørgsmål hørte han intet svar på fra nogen. Spørgsmålet for ham nu var: »Har jeg virkelig ladet Napoleon nå Moskva, og hvornår gjorde jeg det? Hvornår blev det afgjort? Kan det have været i går, da jeg beordrede Platov til at trække sig tilbage, eller var det aftenen forinden, da jeg tog en lur og sagde til Bennigsen, at han skulle udstede ordrer? Eller var det endnu tidligere?... Hvornår, hvornår blev denne frygtelige sag afgjort? Moskva må opgives. Hæren må trække sig tilbage, og ordren til det må gives.« At give den frygtelige ordre forekom ham at svare til at nedlægge kommandoen over hæren. Og ikke alene elskede han magten, som han var vant til (de æresbevisninger, der var tildelt fyrst Prozorovskij, under hvem han havde tjent i Tyrkiet, nagede ham), men han var overbevist om, at han var bestemt til at redde Rusland, og at det netop var derfor, han — mod kejserens ønske og ved folkets vilje — var blevet valgt til øverstkommanderende. Han var overbevist om, at han alene kunne opretholde kommandoen over hæren under disse vanskelige omstændigheder, og at han i hele verden var den eneste, der kunne møde den uovervindelige Napoleon uden frygt, og han gyste ved tanken om den ordre, han måtte give. Men der måtte træffes en afgørelse, og disse samtaler omkring ham, der antog en alt for fri karakter, måtte standses.
Han kaldte de vigtigste generaler til sig.
»Mit hoved, hvad enten det er godt eller dårligt, må stole på sig selv,« sagde han, rejste sig fra bænken og red til Fili, hvor hans vogne ventede.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: When Ermolov, sent by Kutuzov to inspect the position, reported that it was impossible to fight there before Moscow and that they must retreat, Kutuzov looked at him in silence.
"Give me your hand," he said, and turning it over to feel the pulse, added: "You're not well, my dear fellow. Think about what you're saying!"
Kutuzov could not yet bring himself to accept the possibility of retreating beyond Moscow without a battle.

On Poklonny Hill, four miles from the Dorogomilov gate of Moscow, Kutuzov got out of his carriage and sat down on a bench by the roadside. A large group of generals gathered around him, and Count Rostopchin, who had come from Moscow, joined them. This distinguished company split into several groups, all discussing the advantages and disadvantages of the position, the state of the army, the suggested plans, the situation in Moscow, and military matters generally. Though they hadn't been summoned for that purpose and the gathering wasn't officially called one, they all felt this was essentially a council of war. The conversations all dealt with public affairs. If anyone shared or asked for personal news, it was done in a whisper, and they immediately returned to general matters. No jokes, laughter, or even smiles were seen among these men. They all clearly made an effort to rise to the gravity of the situation. And all these groups, while talking among themselves, tried to stay near the commander in chief — whose bench formed the center of the gathering — and to speak loudly enough for him to hear. The commander in chief listened and sometimes asked them to repeat their remarks, but did not join the conversations or express any opinion. After hearing what one group or another had to say, he generally turned away with a look of disappointment, as though they weren't discussing what he wanted to hear. Some debated the chosen position, criticizing not so much the position itself as the competence of those who'd chosen it. Others argued that a mistake had been made earlier — that a battle should have been fought two days ago. Still others talked about the Battle of Salamanca, described by Crosart, a newly arrived Frenchman in a Spanish uniform. (This Frenchman and one of the German princes serving with the Russian army were discussing the siege of Saragossa and whether Moscow could be defended in a similar way.) Count Rostopchin was telling another group that he was prepared to die with the city militia under the capital's walls, but couldn't help regretting having been kept in the dark — had he known sooner, things would have been different. A fifth group, displaying the depth of their strategic thinking, discussed the direction the troops should now take. A sixth group was talking outright nonsense. Kutuzov's expression grew more and more troubled and gloomy. From all this talk he drew only one conclusion: that defending Moscow was physically impossible — in the fullest meaning of those words — so utterly impossible that if some senseless commander were to order a battle, the result would be chaos, not combat. It wouldn't happen because the commanders not only recognized the position as hopeless, but in their conversations were discussing only what would follow its inevitable abandonment. How could commanders lead their troops into battle on ground they considered impossible to hold? The lower-ranking officers and even the soldiers, who also think, considered the position hopeless as well, and therefore could not fight, fully convinced they would be defeated. If Bennigsen insisted on defending the position and others still debated it, the question was no longer important in itself — it merely served as a pretext for argument and intrigue. This Kutuzov understood perfectly.

Bennigsen, who had chosen the position, warmly displayed his Russian patriotism (Kutuzov could not listen to this without wincing) by insisting that Moscow must be defended. His motive was clear as day to Kutuzov: if the defense failed, blame Kutuzov for bringing the army to the Sparrow Hills without fighting; if it succeeded, claim the credit; if no battle were fought, clear himself of blame for abandoning Moscow. But this intrigue no longer occupied the old man. One terrible question consumed him, and he heard no answer from anyone. The question was: "Have I really allowed Napoleon to reach Moscow, and when did I do so? When was it decided? Was it yesterday when I ordered Platov to retreat? Was it the evening before, when I dozed off and told Bennigsen to issue orders? Or was it earlier still? When, when was this terrible thing decided? Moscow must be abandoned. The army must retreat and the order must be given." To give that terrible order felt to him like resigning command of the army. And not only did he love the power he was used to — the honors given to Prince Prozorovsky, under whom he'd served in Turkey, still stung him — but he was convinced he was destined to save Russia, and that was why, against the Emperor's wishes and by the will of the people, he had been chosen commander in chief. He was convinced he alone could keep command of the army in these difficult circumstances, and that he alone in the whole world could face the invincible Napoleon without fear. He was horrified at the thought of the order he had to give. But something had to be decided, and these conversations around him, growing too free, had to be stopped.
He summoned the most important generals to him.
"My head, good or bad, must decide for itself," he said, rising from the bench, and he rode to Fili where his carriages were waiting.
